doc.title: Ann Rabson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 21, 2007

title: Writing a song in her head, a stolen bass lick and listening widely
summary: She composes mentally, writing about not being sad enough for blues, and borrowed a lick from a Texas bass player.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Right. Well we were talking about being stuck for material to write about.

And I thought it was interesting the way you took this idea of like I’m not sad enough to write blues. Okay. So you’re sitting there and you’ve got this idea for a song. Do you sit at the piano and work on it?

No. I can do that in my head. I mean it’s good later on I get to a piano. But I can — night before last there was a song that I do that I was going to try a different rhythm and different pattern with the piano on it. And I lay around and did it in my head. I mean I

have a good musical imagination. This one, I was at somebody’s house. It was at my unfortunately now retired booking agent’s house. And I was whining about, you know I’ve got to write songs for my new album and I’ve got to write songs for a new Saffire album, and I don’t have any ideas. And then I thought maybe I’ll write about that. You know so I remember I had a big yellow pad and I wrote, I think I filled, I don’t know probably the whole pad, and I crossed things out and I’d start again and I’d do — do you know how many rhymes there are with blues? But blues does not have to be sad. I mean it’s almost like the sad stuff makes people feel like they’re not alone and the happy stuff makes them happy. I mean it’s a therapeutic thing. But yeah, no I don’t — writing at the piano, I have to get to piano eventually. But I did, I had that left hand thing in my mind, which is sort of a Memphis thing. Actually I stole it off a bass player from Texas. I — do I dare tell this? Yeah I’ll tell it. I used to, at blues festivals if I heard a bass player who was doing stuff that I was interested in I always had a guitar in my room so I’d invite them up to my room under false pretenses probably and get them to show me what they were doing. And so that’s where I got that little lick there. I think I added a little twirl to it. But yeah, I can think these things pretty well.
Um hum. And then there’s that one sort of chord near the end, which you probably could call a substitution [scats] sort of you just —
Yeah. I mean it’s not a normal 5-4 progression or something.
So is that something that you might just be fooling around with chords that match what you’re trying to sing?
No. It’s something that — I mean I suppose I do that sometimes — most of the time I hear it in my head and I try to find it on the piano.

And I do listen to a lot of different things, which is probably why my music isn’t strictly straight ahead blues, which is, I don’t want to hear just straight-ahead blues, you know? I mean those old guys weren’t playing straight-ahead blues, the people I admire most. They weren’t even playing all major — major and minor at the same time sometimes, and twelve bar blues would become thirteen and eleven. I mean you know, but I listen to everything. I mean I listen to birds, I listen to jazz, I listen to classical, I listen to country, Gospel, I listen to Gospel. You know, so that all goes in and I guess it all comes out too.
